figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: We present ID2Reflectance, a high-quality, identity-conditioned reflectance reconstruction method. ID2Reflectance learns multi-domain face codebooks by using limited captured data and generates multi-view domain-specific reflectance images guided by facial identity. Our approach greatly reduces the dependency on captured data and generates high-fidelity reflectance maps for realistic rendering.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of the proposed method. Our core insight is to build a facial reflectance prior in image space by using limited captures and to recover the reflectance maps for any unconstrained face. We first train multi-domain facial codebooks using a large amount of RGB data and limited reflectance data. Then, given an input unconstrained face, we extract the identity feature from the pre-trained ArcFace [11] model. This feature is fed into the swapper module, which guides the decoder to perform identity injection for all domains. We finally stitch three-view identity-conditioned reflectance images to acquire high-quality rendering assets and renderable 3D faces.
figures.headline: The overview feeds identity features from a pretrained face recognition model into a swapper, and three-view outputs are stitched into renderable assets.

abstract: Recent 3D face reconstruction methods have made remarkable advancements, yet there remain huge challenges in monocular high-quality facial reflectance reconstruction. Existing methods rely on a large amount of light-stage captured data to learn facial reflectance models. However, the lack of subject diversity poses challenges in achieving good generalization and widespread applicability. In this paper, we learn the reflectance prior in image space rather than UV space and present a framework named ID2Reflectance. Our framework can directly estimate the reflectance maps of a single image while using limited reflectance data for training. Our key insight is that reflectance data shares facial structures with RGB faces, which enables obtaining expressive facial prior from inexpensive RGB data thus reducing the dependency on reflectance data. We first learn a high-quality prior for facial reflectance. Specifically, we pretrain multi-domain facial feature codebooks and design a codebook fusion method to align the reflectance and RGB domains. Then, we propose an identity-conditioned swapping module that injects facial identity from the target image into the pre-trained autoencoder to modify the identity of the source reflectance image. Finally, we stitch multi-view swapped reflectance images to obtain renderable assets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method exhibits excellent generalization capability and achieves state-of-the-art facial reflectance reconstruction results for in-the-wild faces. Our project page is https://xingyuren.github.io/id2reflectance/.

sections.body: The introduction states the problem: reflectance models are trained on light-stage data from fewer than three hundred subjects, which limits generalization to real-world identities. The authors instead learn the reflectance prior in image space, where reflectance data shares facial structure with large RGB datasets such as FFHQ. A VQGAN is trained on RGB and reflectance images with multi-domain codebooks. An identity integration module built on AdaIN injects identity from a target face into the pre-trained autoencoder. Three-view reflectance images are then stitched into UV maps. The listed contributions are the multi-domain codebook alignment, a lightweight swapper module, and experiments on in-the-wild faces. This section reports no quantitative results.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Reflectance models trained on few light-stage captures generalize poorly, so the method learns the reflectance prior in image space from abundant RGB faces.

sections.body: Classical 3D Morphable Models use PCA and neglect high-frequency detail, and non-linear variants decode faces from latent vectors. Light-stage captures with polarization separate diffuse and specular reflection, which supports facial reflectance reconstruction. AlbedoMM uses a linear per-vertex color model. AvatarMe++ synthesizes diffuse and specular textures from limited light-stage data. FitMe uses a BRDF generative network with a two-stage fitting method, and Relightify uses a diffusion model. The section notes that the AvatarMe, FitMe and Relightify data are not released. Face-swapping methods are designed for the RGB domain and cannot directly handle reflectance targets. The authors therefore train swapping in RGB with AdaIN identity injection and rely on codebook alignment for transfer.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior facial reflectance methods depend on light-stage data and their data is unreleased, while face swapping methods target only the RGB domain.

sections.body: Stage one trains a VQGAN quantized autoencoder with 1,024 codes of dimension 256 on shared RGB and reflectance data. Stage two freezes the encoder and decoder and fine-tunes five domain-specific codebooks for diffuse albedo, specular albedo, roughness, surface normal and texture. A Swin transformer predicts per-location fusion weights over the five quantized representations. The identity swapper uses parallel branches of convolution and AdaIN blocks inserted into decoder upsampling stages, with identity features from a ResNet-100 ArcFace model. At inference, the closest reflectance template is selected in each of four domains at three views, giving 12 templates. The views are then merged using Deep3D shape estimates and YUV color matching.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Two-stage codebook training aligns reflectance with RGB, so identity swapping learned on RGB transfers to reflectance maps.

sections.body: Implementation uses PyTorch, the Adam optimizer, a batch size of 16 and A6000 GPUs, with images resized to 512 by 512. The captured dataset has 135 participants, of which 115 are used for training and 20 for testing. Stage one trains for 700K iterations at an initial learning rate of 8e-5, and each domain codebook is fine-tuned for 100K iterations. The swapper is trained on 1.77 Million images from 8K identities in VGGFace2HQ. Inference takes 3.8 seconds/face. Qualitative comparisons follow prior work on Digital Emily and in-the-wild images. The authors note minor lipstick artifacts, which they attribute to the VGGFace2HQ data and the GFPGAN restorer. For one tested template, the choice of template changes only the skin tone in diffuse albedo.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Trained on 115 captured subjects, the method gives identity-preserved reflectance on Digital Emily and in-the-wild faces in 3.8 seconds/face.

sections.body: The conclusion describes the method as learning high-quality multi-domain discrete codebooks, which give a reliable reflection prior from limited captured data. Identity features condition the reconstruction of multi-view reflectance images, which are stitched into a complete reflectance map. The authors state that experiments show good qualitative and quantitative performance and excellent generalization to real-world images. The broader impacts paragraph says the method may potentially be abused. It also states the method is intended for high-quality reconstruction and rendering, with applications in faster avatar creation and the metaverse. The section does not add limitations beyond those reported in the experiments.
sections.heading: Conclusions and Discussions
sections.headline: The paper concludes that limited captured data yields a reliable reflectance prior and notes the method could be misused.

sections.body: Appendix A describes the light stage, with 46 12MP DSLR cameras and 5 25MP cameras capturing 15 lighting types in 2 seconds. Appendix B lists FFHQ with 70,000 images, VGGFace2 with over 3.3 million images from over 9000 subjects, and CelebAMask-HQ with 30,000 images. Appendix C gives the codebook settings, with 12 residual blocks in the encoder and 5 resizing layers in the decoder. Appendix D compares swapper configurations, where the chosen F16 + F32 + F64 + F128 reaches 0.965 ID-retrieval and 0.0129 pose error. Appendix E reports a swapping range of approximately -45 to +45 degrees. Table 4 shows diffuse PSNR rising from 25.09 at 30 subjects to 31.62 at 115 subjects. Table 5 reports a total score of 18.43 on the fairness benchmark, described as comparable to other methods.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers the light stage rig, public datasets, codebook and swapper details, UV stitching, a fairness benchmark, and further qualitative results.
